fixes.explanation: Fire is the word. The text says fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed Nadab and Abihu, and they died in the presence of the LORD. Their own fire was in their censers, and this fire came from the LORD's presence. I think this is one of the heavy verses, friend.

Smoke is a reasonable guess, since incense was in those censers. But the text says fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed them. Nadab and Abihu died in the presence of the LORD. I think this is a heavy verse.

Wind is a fair guess, friend, but that's not the word here. The text says fire came out from the presence of the LORD. It consumed Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's sons, and they died in the presence of the LORD. I think this one is heavy.

Around is a fair guess, friend, but it's not the word here. Moses tells Mishael and Elzaphan, sons of Aaron's uncle Uzziel, “carry the bodies of your cousins outside the camp, away from the front of the sanctuary.” The word is outside, and they carry them out as Moses had directed. I think this was a hard job to be handed.

The text says the opposite, friend. Moses tells Aaron and his sons Eleazar and Ithamar, “Do not let your hair become disheveled and do not tear your garments, or else you will die…” So True is the answer, because they are told not to tear their garments. The verse goes on to say the LORD will be angry with the whole congregation.

That's it. Moses says, “But your brothers, the whole house of Israel, may mourn on account of the fire that the LORD has ignited.” Notice the contrast. Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar are told not to let their hair become disheveled or tear their garments, while the whole house of Israel may mourn.

No one in the camp doesn't match what Moses says, friend. First he tells Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar not to let their hair become disheveled or tear their garments. Then he turns to the others: “But your brothers, the whole house of Israel, may mourn…” Mourning is open to all of Israel.

Yes. The LORD tells Aaron, “You and your sons are not to drink wine or strong drink when you enter the Tent of Meeting, or else you will die; this is a permanent statute for the generations to come.” Listen to that last part: “for the generations to come.” That's a rule with no expiration date, unlike the coupon I once shared a junk drawer with, which had one and believed in itself anyway.

Counting people makes sense as a priest's job, friend, but it isn't in this verse. The LORD tells Aaron to distinguish between the holy and the common, and the clean and the unclean, “…so that you may teach the Israelites all the statutes that the LORD has given them through Moses.” The reason He gives is teaching. The priests are the ones who pass those statutes along.

Angry is right. Moses searches carefully for the goat of the sin offering and finds it burned up. The text says “He was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron’s remaining sons…” Then he asks them why they didn't eat it in the holy place.

That's the question. Aaron says, “Behold, this very day they presented their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD.” Then he adds that these things have happened to him, and asks, “…if I had eaten the sin offering today, would it have been acceptable in the sight of the LORD?”

Satisfied is right. The text says, “And when Moses heard this explanation, he was satisfied.” Back in verse 16 he was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar. After Aaron's explanation, the text says he was satisfied.
